lesson.title: Calling Something a Continuous Function: What the Label Really Promises
lesson.summary: When mathematicians call f simply a continuous function, without naming an interval, they mean f is continuous at every point of its domain, which lets whole families of familiar functions earn the label at once.
lesson.body:
So far continuity has been attached to a point or to a named interval. The phrase continuous function, used without any interval attached, means something slightly different and slightly more sweeping: f is continuous at every point of its domain. The domain is doing important work in that sentence. A continuous function is not required to be defined everywhere, and it is not required to behave well at points outside its domain, since those points are not part of the promise at all. It only has to pass the continuity test at every point where it is actually defined.

This is why entire families of functions can be declared continuous as a blanket fact. Every polynomial is continuous on all of the real numbers, because polynomials are built from addition and multiplication of continuous pieces, x and constants, and both operations preserve continuity. Every rational function, a quotient of two polynomials, is continuous on its domain, which is every real number except the finitely many where the denominator is zero. The functions sin(x) and cos(x) are continuous on all of the real numbers, and sqrt(x) is continuous on [0, infinity), the largest set of inputs where it is even defined.

Worked example: let f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2). The domain of f excludes x = 2, since the denominator vanishes there, so the domain is all real numbers except 2. Because f is a rational function, it is continuous at every point of that domain: for any c not equal to 2, lim(x to c) f(x) = f(c) by the quotient rule for limits, since the denominator c - 2 is nonzero. So f qualifies as a continuous function, full stop, even though it has no value at x = 2 at all. There is no contradiction here, since x = 2 was never part of the domain, so there was never a promise to keep there.

Compare that with a piecewise function that is defined everywhere but still fails to be continuous. Let g(x) = x for x not equal to 3, and g(3) = 10. This function has all of the real numbers as its domain, including x = 3. Checking continuity at that point, lim(x to 3) g(x) = 3, since g(x) = x for every x near 3 other than 3 itself, but g(3) = 10, so the limit does not match the function value. Because x = 3 is inside the domain and the test fails there, g is not a continuous function, unlike the rational function f above whose only trouble spot was excluded from its domain from the start.

The distinction matters in practice: before you can call something a continuous function, first identify its domain honestly, then check that every point of that domain passes the continuity test. Missing this order is a common source of confusion, since it is tempting to think a formula like 1/x is discontinuous, when the more careful statement is that 1/x is a continuous function on its natural domain, the real numbers excluding zero, precisely because zero was never part of what the function promised to handle.
